w: Bishop Edward Steere laid out the design; built 1873-1879 on ground that once held Zanzibar's largest slave market. The altar is said to mark the spot of the market's whipping post, and the cathedral was consecrated in 1903 to mark the end of slavery. Steere died just before completion.
s: An altar built on the site of the old whipping post
_facts: Anglican cathedral in Stone Town, built 1873-1879 to a design contributed to by Bishop Edward Steere, consecrated 1903
Built on the site of Zanzibar's largest former slave market; altar said to mark the location of the market's whipping post
Steere died shortly before completion and is buried behind the altar

w: Built in 1904 by Bomanjee Maneckjee for Sultan Ali bin Hamud, this is the biggest bazaar in Stone Town, still known locally as Estella Market, after the sister of a former prime minister of Zanzibar. Extended and restored since, it deals mostly in seafood, meat, fruit, grain and spices, plus clothing and electronics.
s: Stone Town's main bazaar, also called Estella Market
_facts: Main bazaar of Stone Town, built 1904 by Bomanjee Maneckjee for Sultan Ali bin Hamud
Also known as Estella Market, after Countess Estella, sister of Lloyd Mathews (Prime Minister of Zanzibar)
Primarily a food market (seafood, meat, fruit, grain, spices) with other goods sold alongside

w: Sultan Barghash bin Said commissioned Shirazi architects to build these public baths between 1870 and 1888, hence Hamamni, place of the baths. Aqueducts carried hot water for men and women on separate schedules, though only the wealthy could really afford it. They closed around 1920, restored by volunteers in 2006.
s: Persian-style public baths, built for a sultan
_facts: Public baths built 1870-1888 for Sultan Barghash bin Said, designed by Shirazi (Persian) architects
Used underground aqueducts for hot water; separate admittance hours for men and women
Ceased operating around 1920; restored by CHAM volunteers in 2006

w: This Roman Catholic cathedral counts among Stone Town's most important historical buildings and draws visitors as readily as worshippers. Several masses are held here every Sunday, with occasional weekday services too, so tourists wander in to admire the architecture and end up sharing pews with the local congregation.
s: A working Catholic cathedral and a landmark both
_facts: Roman Catholic cathedral, one of the most important historical buildings and visitor attractions in Stone Town
Regularly used by the local Catholic community, with several Sunday masses and occasional weekday services

w: This three-storey palace with merlon-decorated white walls replaced an earlier one, Bait As-Sahel, destroyed in the 1896 Anglo-Zanzibar War. Renamed the People's Palace after 1964, it became a museum in 1994, its floors devoted to Sultan Khalifa bin Harub and Princess Sayyida Salme, who fled to Hamburg as Emily Ruete.
s: The sultan's home, then the people's, now a museum
_facts: Palace Museum on Mizingani Road, built late 19th century on the site of the earlier Bait As-Sahel palace destroyed in the 1896 Anglo-Zanzibar War
Renamed People's Palace in 1964 after the Zanzibar Revolution; became a museum in 1994
Exhibits cover Sultan Khalifa bin Harub and Princess Sayyida Salme (Emily Ruete), who relocated to Hamburg

w: Also known as the Arab Fort, this is the oldest surviving building in Stone Town and one of its biggest draws, standing on the seafront next to the old Sultan's palace, the House of Wonders, and facing straight onto the Forodhani Gardens. A fortification once, a tourist landmark now, it anchors the waterfront.
s: Stone Town's oldest building, right on the seafront
_facts: Fortification in Stone Town, also called the Arab Fort; oldest building and a major visitor attraction of Stone Town
Located on the main seafront, adjacent to the House of Wonders and facing the Forodhani Gardens

w: Also called Jubilee Gardens, this seafront park faces Stone Town's two most famous buildings, the House of Wonders and the Old Fort, and comes alive after dark when a market fills the square with grilled seafood and samosas. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture rehabilitated it from 2009, rebuilding seawall and walkways.
s: A seafront park that turns into a night food market
_facts: Seafront park in Stone Town, also known as Jubilee Gardens, facing the House of Wonders and the Old Fort
Nightly food market sells grilled seafood, samosas, cassava and sweet potato
Rehabilitated by the Aga Khan Trust for Culture, ground-breaking in July 2009

w: Also known as the Ithnashiri Dispensary, this building served as a dispensary through the early twentieth century and remains one of Stone Town's most ornate structures. Its carved wooden balconies with stained glass show Indian influence, atop a coral rag and limestone frame finished in neo-classical stucco.
s: A dispensary building fancier than most cathedrals
_facts: Historic building in Stone Town, also called the Ithnashiri Dispensary, served as a dispensary in the early-to-mid 20th century
Carved wooden balconies with stained glass in an Indian-influenced style; structure of coral rag and limestone with neo-classical stucco
Now houses a small museum on Zanzibar's history

w: Standing on its own island off Zanzibar's coast, this lighthouse burned acetylene gas for decades, its flame automated since 1926 by a sun valve that lit it at dusk with nobody there to do it. It finally went solar in 2013, swapping gas for photovoltaic panels while keeping the same job it always had.
s: A 19th-century lighthouse running on solar power now
_facts: Historic lighthouse on Chumbe Island, Zanzibar
Burned acetylene until 2013, automated by a sun valve since 1926
Converted to a solar-powered (photovoltaic) light system in 2013
